catalog_quote: 1.3.1. Stress. Word-level stress falls on the final syllable if closed, which is the case for most words (17a). For the small set of words (mostly function words and recent borrowings) which end in an open syllable, stress falls on the penult (17b). (17a) Stress on final closed syllable n′i|p′i|lán ‘people’, la|ków ‘guava’, ᵐbo|wɨp′ ‘raccoon’, kah|ᵐb′íəl ‘wasp’, eʦ′ |w′ǽk ‘monkey’ (17b) Stress on penult when final syllable is open n′í |n′e ‘child’, i|kó|ɾa ‘we incl. dual’, kʷá|n′e ‘what?’ This stress pattern is consistent with a number of formal metrical analyses. Because the choice among these has no effect on the following discussion, I leave aside further discussion of these. ... [sec. 3.1.1, ms pp. 59-62] 3.1.1. Stress. As already introduced in §1.3.1, stress falls on the word-final syllable if it is closed, otherwise on the penult. Stress assignment rules apply both cyclically and non-cyclically in derived forms ... When the stresses are not adjacent, the final one becomes the primary stress of the word and the preceding stress is demoted to a secondary stress, as in tahɨn′ ì:ʦ′asán .

sweep_summary: sanm1287 (San Mateo del Mar Huave) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Aguilar Ruiz 2019 (Colmex PhD, 241 pp.), was already held by the project from an earlier reading of this compilation and was re-read: sec. 2.4 'Patrón acentual' (pp. 56-57) gives an explicit word-stress generalization — stress on the first heavy (closed) syllable from the right, i.e. the final syllable in nearly all words, and on the penult in the few open-final function words and Spanish loans (nine, xike, ike, buelta). This matches Noyer 2013 IJAL sec. 1.3.1 (final if closed, else penult), Evanini 2007 BLS (instrumental confirmation, pp. 54-55) and Pak 2007 BLS (p. 312, in passing); Stairs & Hollenbach 1981 p. 285 note only that stress migrates to a monosyllabic suffix. Noyer 2013 is the most authoritative statement; Aguilar Ruiz 2019 is the best open-access one with clean page numbers. The Colmex direct PDF link was verified live (HTTP 200). Noyer's dictionary web intro was downloaded and is silent on stress. Not obtained: Noyer 1991 ESCOL (low priority; superseded by Noyer 2013), the full Stairs & Stairs 1981 dictionary front matter (low). Recommended coding if added: fixed right-edge stress, weight-sensitive (final closed syllable, else penult); tone contrast confined to the stressed syllable. updated at

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is on the final syllable, which in native vocabulary is (almost) always closed; the handful of words ending in an open (CV) syllable — some pronouns/function words and recent Spanish loans — stress the penult instead. Equivalent weight formulation (Aguilar Ruiz 2019, Pak 2007): stress the rightmost heavy (closed) syllable, else the penult. Lexical tone (H vs HL) is contrastive only on the stressed syllable and is realized phrasally.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Noyer sec. 3.1.1: stress is assigned cyclically in derived (suffixed) verbs; when an earlier cycle's stress is not adjacent to the word-final primary stress it survives as a secondary stress (e.g. tahɨn′ ì:ʦ′asán 'we excl. cooked'), and when adjacent it is removed by Stress Clash Deletion (tahawás 'I saw'). No rhythmic secondary stress is described.
new_statements.exceptions: Words ending in an open syllable (mostly function words such as n′ín′e 'child', ikóɾa 'we', kʷán′e 'what?', xíkè 'I', and recent loans such as nínè 'baby', bèjúgò 'vine') take penultimate stress; enclitics (e.g. #an, #a) are never stressed (sec. 2.5.2); one-syllable suffixes attract the stress off the root (Stairs & Hollenbach 1981 sec. 0.1).
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly 'word-level stress' on citation/isolated word forms including inflected verbs; enclitics fall outside the stress domain. Tone (H/HL) is a separate, largely phrasal system whose contrasts surface only on syllables bearing phrase-level stress (Noyer sec. 1.3.3; Pike & Warkentin 1961). San Mateo is the only Huave variety retaining tone.
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted sources describe the San Mateo del Mar variety specifically (Noyer's title 'San Mateo Huave'; Aguilar Ruiz, Evanini and Pak all worked with San Mateo del Mar speakers), i.e. exactly sanm1287 [huv]. San Mateo is the only one of the four Huave varieties that retains lexical tone (Noyer 2013 sec. 1.3.3); the sister varieties San Francisco del Mar (sanf1258, Kim 2008), San Dionisio del Mar (sand1278) and Santa María del Mar (sant1422) are separate Glottolog languages and are not covered by this statement.

new_statements.quote: 1. Normalmente, las palabras que terminan en consonante llevan el acento en la última sílaba (aun cuando terminen en n o s). Por ejemplo: aráng hace, andiümǘw quieren, tarangás hice, tarangasán hicimos. 2. Cuando un sufijo o sufijos forman dos o más sílabas, la raíz conserva un acento secundario además del primario que va en la última sílaba. Por ejemplo: aquíiüb acompaña, aquíiübaranáats nos acompañaron. [p. xvii] ... Cuando el enclítico -an solamente se agrega a una palabra, la raíz conserva el acento, y éste se escribe, por ejemplo, andeac habla, andeácan solamente habla. [p. xviii]
new_statements.translation: 1. Normally, words ending in a consonant carry the stress on the last syllable (even when they end in n or s). For example: aráng 'does', andiümǘw 'they want', tarangás 'I did', tarangasán 'we did'. 2. When a suffix or suffixes form two or more syllables, the root keeps a secondary stress in addition to the primary one, which goes on the last syllable. For example: aquíiüb 'accompanies', aquíiübaranáats 'they accompanied us'. [p. xvii] ... When the enclitic -an 'only' is added to a word, the root keeps the stress, and this is written, e.g. andeac 'speaks', andeácan 'only speaks'. [p. xviii]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing statements (Noyer 2013: final if closed; Aguilar Ruiz 2019; Evanini 2007) — final stress on consonant-final words, i.e. nearly all words. Adds a secondary stress on the root under polysyllabic suffixation and the unstressed enclitic -an, matching Noyer's cyclic secondary stress and 'enclitics never stressed'. The catalog record for sanm1287 itself has an empty rule field; this source supports filling it as fixed: final syllable.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words ending in a consonant (the normal case) are stressed on the last syllable; stress is written only where it departs from this pattern. When suffixation adds two or more syllables the root keeps a secondary stress, the primary staying final. The enclitic -an 'only' does not take stress (the root keeps it). Tone: two tones (agudo/grave) distinguish only three word pairs and are not.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated explicitly: with two or more suffix syllables the root keeps a secondary stress beside the final primary (aquíiüb -> aquíiübaranáats). Cf. Apéndice A 'Gramática huave' 0.1 p. 285 (already held by the project): a one-syllable suffix takes the stress from the root.
new_statements.exceptions: Rule stated only for consonant-final words ('Normalmente.. que terminan en consonante'); vowel-final words are not addressed in this section beyond the note that stress is written when it deviates. Enclitic -an is unstressed (andeácan). Stress is also written to resolve vowel-sequence ambiguities (anaíw, aíum) and to distinguish homographs (aag vs áag).
new_statements.identity_note: Work 0 (Kim 2008) describes San Francisco del Mar Huave (Glottolog sanf1258), not San Mateo del Mar; it is on this item's list only because it cites the San Mateo literature. Work 1 (Stairs & Stairs 1981) is explicitly the San Mateo del Mar variety (title). The San Mateo dialect is the only Huave variety with a (marginal) lexical tone contrast: two tones distinguishing three word pairs per Stairs & Stairs p. xvii.

sources.note: Sec. 1.3.1 (ms pp. 24-25): word-level stress falls on the final syllable if closed (most words); the small set of words ending in an open syllable (mostly function words and recent loans) stress the penult. Sec. 2.5.2: enclitics are never stressed. Sec. 3.1.1 (ms pp. 59-62): stress applies cyclically; an earlier cyclic stress non-adjacent to the final stress survives as secondary (tahɨn' ì:ts'asán), an adjacent one is deleted (Stress Clash Deletion). Sec. 1.3.3: lexical tone (H vs HL) surfaces only on phrase-stressed syllables; San Mateo is the only Huave dialect retaining tone.

sources.quote: En los ejemplos de (8) se puede observar que el acento cae en la primera sílaba con coda, de derecha a izquierda. [...] Sin embargo, en un reducido conjunto de palabras funcionales y en algunos préstamos del español, como se muestra en (10), el acento recae sobre la penúltima sílaba cuando la palabra no termina en coda. [...] (4) GENERALIZACIÓN SOBRE LA POSICIÓN DEL ACENTO: el acento cae sobre la primera sílaba pesada, de derecha a izquierda; sin embargo, cuando en la palabra no hay sílaba pesada, el acento recae sobre la penúltima sílaba ligera. Es decir, el acento en huave es predecible, se asigna en la primera sílaba pesada CVC, CVVC o CV1V2C, de derecha a izquierda.
sources.note: Sec. 2.4 'Patrón acentual' (pp. 56-57): stress falls on the first heavy (closed: CVC, CVVC, CV1V2C) syllable counting from the right; Spanish loans adapt the same way (ma.'tʃet, man.'san, 'buel.ta); a small set of function words and some loans ending in an open syllable stress the penult ('ni.ne, 'ʃi.ke, 'i.ke). Generalization (4): 'el acento cae sobre la primera sílaba pesada, de derecha a izquierda.. cuando en la palabra no hay sílaba pesada, el acento recae sobre la penúltima sílaba ligera'. Sec. 2.5-2.6: lexical H/HL contrast only on the stressed syllable; tone depends on stress.

sources.citation: Evanini, Keelan. 2007. The phonetic realization of pitch accent in Huave. Proceedings of the 33rd Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society 33(2): 53-64. doi:10.3765/bls.v33i2.3501.
sources.quote: The metrical structure of Huave is straightforward: all final syllables are closed and bear pitch accent whereas all other syllables are unaccented and receive L. Thus, the contrast between H and HL is only found on final syllables. [...] A small number of words are exceptional in that they allow final open syllables. In these cases, the accent falls on the penult, and the final syllable receives L. These cases are limited to certain pronouns, such as xíkè 'I' and ìkórà 'we', and borrowed words, such as nínè 'baby' and bèjúgò 'vine'.
sources.locator: sec. 1 'Tone and Metrical Structure', p. 54; sec. 1.2 'Exceptions', p. 55

sources.quote: A Phrasal H tone docks on the primary-stressed (final if heavy, else penultimate) syllable of the 'head' of the phrase. If this syllable already has Lexical L, then a HL contour tone is produced ((6)b).
